setting: a veterinary telehealth startup adding a 24-hour triage line (Burrow Vet Online)
prompt: I need you to stress‑test the proposal I’m taking to Dr. Maya Patel, our CEO at Burrow Vet Online. We plan to launch a 24‑hour triage line on 2025‑03‑01, staffed initially by three licensed veterinarians and two support nurses. Our budget shows $250,000 in staffing and technology costs, plus a $45,000 marketing push, but the spreadsheet mistakenly adds the two figures as $280,000 instead of $295,000. We project 1,200 calls per month in the first quarter, assuming 80 % will be resolved without an in‑person referral and generate $12 per call in revenue, yielding $144,000 quarterly. The unknown is the average handling time per call, which could affect how many calls each clinician can take. Also, we haven’t priced the potential regulatory compliance fees, which could be $30,000–$50,000. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to go ahead, outline the three biggest ways this rollout could fail (including the hidden cost slip and the handling‑time uncertainty), and tell me what specific metric—like sustained call abandonment above 15 % or a net loss of $50k in the first two months—should trigger us to stop or pivot. Thanks.

setting: a meal-kit company moving fulfillment to a second warehouse (Saltbox Kitchens)
prompt: I’m drafting a proposal to move a portion of our fulfillment from the current 70,000‑sq‑ft Boston hub to a second warehouse we’ve called Saltbox Kitchens in Albany. The plan is to shift 35% of weekly orders—about 1,400 pallets (assuming 4,000 pallets total) by the start of Q4 2024. We estimate the Albany lease at $12.50 per sq‑ft, giving us $437,500 annual rent versus the Boston site’s $7.80 per sq‑ft ($546,000). We’re counting a labor saving of $150,000 per year because the new site is 15 minutes closer to 60% of our supplier base, reducing inbound mileage by 500 miles per day. The assumption is that the build‑out will be completed by 15 Oct 2024 and that we can staff the new location with the same hourly rate of $22. The unknown is the cost to upgrade the automated picking system at Saltbox; the vendor quote has not arrived yet. I need this stress‑tested for Maya Patel, our CEO. Please give me one clear recommendation, outline the biggest ways this could fail, and tell me the specific result (e.g., if labor savings fall below $70k or rent exceeds $600k) that would make us stop or pivot.

setting: a solar installer launching a battery-storage upsell (Meridian Roofline Energy)
prompt: I need you to stress‑test the upsell plan I’m taking to Maya Patel, our CFO, next week. We’re launching Meridian Roofline Energy’s battery‑storage add‑on for residential solar installs. The proposal assumes we can bundle the battery for $120,000 per house (including hardware, permitting and a 3‑year service contract) and still hit a 15 % gross margin because the hardware cost is $102,000. We currently install about 200 systems per quarter and expect 30 % of those customers to add the battery, giving us roughly 60 upsells per quarter. The model projects $7.2 M in additional revenue by Q3 2025, with a payback period of 4.2 years for the customer based on a 20 % reduction in grid charges. The assumption is that permitting will never exceed two weeks per site. I still don’t know the exact insurance premium for the batteries, and I’m not sure how seasonal temperature swings will affect the battery’s degradation rate. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to move forward, the three most likely ways this could fail, and the specific result (e.g., if the actual margin falls below 10 % or if churn among upsell customers exceeds 12 % in the first six months) that would trigger us to kill or redesign the program.

setting: a property-management firm piloting smart locks across 800 units (Keystone Hollow Properties)
prompt: I’m preparing a proposal for our COO, Ravi Singh, to move from the current pilot of smart locks to a full‑scale rollout across all 800 Keystone Hollow Properties units. The pilot began on 10 Jan 2024 with 100 locks at $120 each (we’ve recorded a total spend of $10,500, though the math suggests $12,000). So far we’ve seen a 30% drop in maintenance calls and an estimated $180,000 in annual savings, assuming the 90% tenant adoption rate we projected. The plan is to install the remaining 700 locks by Q3 2025 at the same $120 price, which would bring total hardware spend to $84,000 plus an unknown integration cost with our leasing platform. Our assumption is that the existing Wi‑Fi network can handle the extra 800 devices without upgrades, and we’re banking on a two‑year battery life. I need you to give me one clear recommendation on whether to go ahead, list the three biggest ways this could fail (including any hidden cost or risk you spot), and state the specific result—such as a tenant satisfaction drop below 70% or a 15% increase in service tickets—that would trigger us to kill the project. The answer is for Ravi to present at the next leadership meeting.

setting: a language-learning app testing a family plan (Tidepool Tongues)
prompt: I need you to stress‑test the family plan proposal before I pitch it to Maya Patel, our CEO. Tidepool Tongues has 12,000 active paid users as of March 31 2024, and we’re planning a Family Plan at $4.99 per month for up to four members. We assume 20 % of the current user base will upgrade within the first six months, giving us roughly 2,400 families. The projected annual revenue is $150,000 (2,400 × $4.99 × 12), which we compare to our existing individual subscription revenue of $130,000, claiming a 20 % increase. Development cost is budgeted at $150,000, and we’ve allocated $25,000 for marketing, but we haven’t priced the additional customer‑support load. The launch is set for July 15 2024, with a three‑month pilot in two regions. Unknowns: the churn rate for family accounts and the price sensitivity of parents with kids under 12. I want you to give Maya one clear recommendation, list the main ways the plan could fail, and tell me the specific metric (e.g., ≤5 % conversion after the pilot) that would trigger us to stop or pivot.

setting: a physical-therapy clinic group launching an app-based home-exercise program (Ironbark Physio)
prompt: I’m putting together a pitch for our co‑founder Maya Patel about the Ironbark Physio home‑exercise app, and I need it stress‑tested before I walk into the exec meeting. We would start development on 1 May 2025, earmark $120,000 for design, testing and a 12‑month pilot that launches on 1 Oct 2025. Our target is to sign up at least 500 patients, each paying $30 per month, which we project as $15,000 in monthly revenue. We assume a 70 % adherence rate will keep churn under 5 % and that the app will cut in‑clinic visits by roughly 10 % for those users. The real unknown is the timeline for the state health board to certify the app for remote prescription – we have no firm deadline. I need you to give Maya one clear recommendation on whether to move forward, identify the three biggest ways this plan could fail, and specify the pre‑agreed kill‑switch condition (for example, if monthly sign‑ups dip below 30 after the first three months). Also flag any hidden cost or risk you notice.

setting: a regional trucking broker building its own load-matching tool (Cinder Mile Freight)
prompt: I’m preparing a proposal for Maya Patel, our COO, to get approval for building a proprietary load‑matching platform for Cinder Mile Freight. We would spend $450,000 on initial development over a six‑month sprint and another $85,000 to integrate with three carrier APIs. The model assumes our current broker commission stays at 15% and that we will handle 3,200 loads per month, each averaging $250 in revenue, giving us $800,000 in monthly gross. We project a 12% internal rate of return over the next 24 months and expect to break even in 18 months, with ongoing ops and support costing $30,000 per month. The only cost I haven’t nailed down is the licensing fee for the national carrier data feed; estimates range from $10,000 to $25,000 per year. I also compared this to a competitor’s off‑the‑shelf tool that cost $200,000 upfront, but I didn’t factor their subscription fees. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to push this forward, list the three biggest ways the plan could fail (including any hidden risks you spot), and specify the pre‑agreed trigger that would make us kill the project (e.g., if a key metric isn’t met by a certain date).

setting: a farm-to-table restaurant group opening a catering arm (Thistledown Table)
prompt: Maya Patel, our COO, will decide next week whether we move forward with the catering arm of Thistledown Table. I need you to stress‑test the proposal I’m about to present. We plan to launch on July 15, 2025, with a $150,000 upfront investment for a mobile prep unit, a $35,000 lease on a satellite kitchen, and $20,000 for branding. Our model assumes we can handle an extra 20 % load on the existing kitchen without adding staff, and that the 12 % food‑cost margin we enjoy in the restaurant will hold for catering. We project 150 corporate events in the first twelve months at an average ticket of $2,000, which should generate $300,000 in revenue and cover the $250,000 total cost, leaving a modest profit. The unknown is the actual demand for corporate catering in the 30‑mile radius around our flagship location. Please give me: one clear recommendation on whether to proceed, the three most likely ways this plan could fail, and the specific result (e.g., fewer than 80 events in the first six months) that would trigger us to stop or pivot.

setting: a podcast studio network launching a paid members tier (Hollybrook Audio)
prompt: I’m drafting the proposal for our new paid‑members tier and need it stress‑tested before I present it to CEO Maya Patel on Thursday. We plan to launch in Q4 2024 with a monthly price of $9.99 and anticipate 5,000 members by the end of the first 12 months, which would generate roughly $600,000 in revenue (5,000 × $9.99 × 12 ≈ $599,400). The platform integration will cost $150,000 up front, and we’re budgeting $80,000 for marketing, $45,000 for added bandwidth, and $30,000 for a part‑time community manager—costs we haven’t fully factored into the P&L yet. Our assumption is that we can convert 2% of our current 250,000 free listeners, based on a similar podcast’s experience, but we have no data on churn after the first three months (the unknown). We’ve also compared our model to a competitor who charges $15/month and reports an 8% churn rate, yet we haven’t accounted for their larger audience of 1.2 million listeners. Please give me: one clear recommendation on whether to move forward; the three biggest ways this plan could fail; and the specific metric or result that would trigger us to stop or pivot the tier.

setting: a hardware store co-op creating a private-label paint line (Anvil and Oak Co-op)
prompt: I need a quick stress‑test of the private‑label paint launch I’m taking to Maya Patel, our co‑op chairman, next week. We plan to spend $2.5 million on a small‑batch line, using our existing bottling line to fill 12,000 gallons in the first year at $24 per gallon, which we think will give us a 28 % gross margin. The rollout is scheduled for 9 months after the RFP close on 15 Mar 2025, with production starting 1 Oct 2025. My key assumption is that our current distribution network can absorb the extra volume with no additional logistics cost. The unknown is how the new formula will hold up in high‑humidity climates; we haven’t done a full field test yet. I also realized I estimated a break‑even point at month 8 based on a $500 k profit target, but I didn’t factor in a 12 % marketing surcharge we’ll need for trade‑show presence. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to go ahead, list the main ways this plan could fail (including any hidden cost or risk you spot), and tell me the exact trigger that would make us stop or change course—e.g., if Q1 sales dip below 3,000 gallons or if total cost overruns exceed 15 % of budget. Thanks.

setting: an HR-software vendor adding an AI interview-scheduling assistant (Plumline HR)
prompt: I’m preparing a pitch for Maya Patel, our COO, to add an AI interview‑scheduling assistant called Plumline HR to our product suite. We currently serve 3,500 enterprise clients and generate $12 million in revenue. The development budget is $1.8 million, with a nine‑month timeline (July 2025‑March 2026). I’m assuming a 30 % reduction in recruiter admin time will translate into $500 k annual cost savings for the average client, based on the $60 hour rate we’ve quoted. We expect to charge a $2 per‑seat monthly add‑on, which should bring $840 k in ARR after the first year if we reach a 15 % adoption rate among existing customers. The unknown is the regulatory environment for AI‑driven scheduling in the US and EU; we have no clear guidance yet. I need you to give Maya one clear recommendation on whether to proceed, list the main ways this rollout could fail (including any hidden cost or risk you spot), and state the pre‑agreed condition that would make us kill the project or pivot.

setting: a bicycle manufacturer reshoring frame production (Kestrel Spoke Cycles)
prompt: I need you to stress‑test the reshoring proposal I’m about to pitch to our CFO, Maya Patel, next Tuesday. We plan to close our current frame contract in Vietnam by 30 June 2025 and bring the stamping line in‑house at our Dayton plant. The capital outlay is $2.5 million, which we’ve broken down as $1.9 M for new presses, $400 k for tooling, and $200 k for facility upgrades. We estimate an annual production of 150,000 frames, a 30 % increase in lead‑time reliability, and a 12‑month ramp‑up period. Our model assumes labor cost stays flat at $22 per hour for the next three years, and we’ve priced the saved import duty at $0 because we think the current tariff on aluminum will be removed by 2026. The expected margin improvement is 5 percentage points, yielding an extra $1.1 M in profit over five years. The unknown is the exact future tariff rate if the duty remains. Also, we didn’t factor the $300 k cost of retraining the existing workforce. Please give me: one clear recommendation on whether to proceed, the three biggest ways this plan could fail, and the specific result (e.g., profit shortfall or lead‑time degradation) that would trigger us to kill or radically change the project.

setting: an urgent-care clinic chain extending hours to midnight (Willowmere Urgent Care)
prompt: Hi, I’m Sam, Operations Lead at Willowmere Urgent Care. I’m preparing a proposal for Dr. Maya Patel, our COO, to extend clinic hours to midnight at three locations (Maple, Oak, and Pine). We project an additional 180 patient visits per month across the three sites, averaging $85 per visit, which I calculated as $14,000 extra revenue per month. The pilot would start on 2024-11-01 and run for six months. I assume the increased hours will boost overall market share by 10% and that existing staff can cover the night shift with a $250,000 budget for overtime and new hires. The unknown is the exact cost of night‑shift security and utilities, which we haven’t quoted yet. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to move forward, list the three biggest ways this could fail, and tell me the specific metric or event that would trigger us to stop or re‑evaluate the plan. The trigger we discussed is if net profit from the midnight hours falls below $3,000 per month for two consecutive months.

setting: a children's museum considering a traveling exhibit program (Pennywhistle Museum)
prompt: I’m drafting a brief for Ms. Lila Hart, our board chair, and need your help stress‑testing the traveling exhibit proposal before our June 1 2025 kickoff. We plan to launch the “World of Wonder” pop‑up in five cities—Portland (June 1–14), Austin (June 20–July 3), Denver (July 10–23), Charlotte (August 1–14), and Milwaukee (August 20–September 2). Each site will run for two weeks, with an estimated 3,500 visitors per city at $12 per ticket, which we’ve tallied as $210,000 total revenue (3,500 × 5 × $12). The exhibit build‑out costs $150,000, logistics (crating, trucking, and staff travel) are budgeted at $30,000 per city, and we assume a 30 % conversion of visitors into new museum members. The only cost we haven’t quantified is the insurance premium, which the carrier says is “subject to final underwriting.” I want one clear recommendation on whether to move forward, the three biggest ways this could fail, and the pre‑agreed trigger that would make us cancel or re‑scope (e.g., if early ticket sales fall below a certain threshold). Please spot any arithmetic or assumption flaws that a careful reviewer would catch.

setting: a boutique accounting firm launching fixed-fee bookkeeping subscriptions (Juniper Ledger LLP)
prompt: I need you to stress‑test the rollout plan I’m taking to our managing partner, Elena Vasquez, next Thursday. Juniper Ledger LLP will launch three fixed‑fee bookkeeping subscription tiers on 15 Oct 2024: Basic at $149/month, Professional at $299/month, and Enterprise at $599/month. We project 120‑month‑old clients will move to Professional, and that we’ll add 85 new Basic clients and 40 new Enterprise clients each month for the first six months. The model assumes a 5 % churn rate and that the average upsell will be $120 per client per year. We’ve budgeted $45,000 for the SaaS integration, but I haven’t been able to get a firm quote on the API usage fees, which could be a variable cost. The revenue forecast adds the six‑month numbers to $2.34 M, but I suspect I may have double‑counted the Enterprise upsells. I want one clear recommendation on whether to proceed, the three biggest ways this could fail (including any hidden cost or mis‑calculation), and the specific metric—if net new ARR falls below $150k after month 3—that would trigger us to halt the program or pivot to a per‑hour model. Please keep the answer focused for Elena.
